before.name: Drakenspire Portals
before.basicInfo:
Drakenspire's portalward quarter is the usual first stop in the snowy capital. An enclosed basalt transit hall opens into a compact market and communal hearth court; beyond them, steep lanes connect the lower city's homes and workshops. Above the roofs to the northeast, the fortress rises within the immense crescent of the ancestral dragon's bones. Travelers can arrange cargo, buy a hot meal, obtain directions and hear current road conditions before choosing where to go. This map location covers the arrival quarter; the wider city and nation also bear the name Drakenspire.

People associated with this place include: Fuyumi Kirihara — Portal arrivals clerk; Daigo Numata — Portal cargo porter.

The lanes lead into the lower city, while an uphill view repeatedly catches the fortress bones through gaps between chimneys.

A torn packing label may require the owner to identify a crate; opening it or taking its contents is a separate matter. Daigo Numata is usually based here, working as portal cargo porter.

Red pennants snap above the entrance while a broad stream of students climbs toward Phoenix Wing Academy. Returning students call to friends across the court; first-years keep glancing between the doors and the papers in their hands. Somewhere behind the practice wall, a whistle cuts through the clack of wooden blades. The breakfast stall by the steps is doing excellent business with people who insist they are not late.

The registrar's desk has been set just inside the Main Hall. A clerk checks the new student's name against the admitted list, passes over a folded timetable, and points to the waiting benches. Admission is settled. Today is about finding the right room.

Hinae Komori moves aside to make space, holding her own timetable flat with both hands.

“I checked the room number three times. I still nearly followed the second-years.”

A bell sounds. The conversations travel into the hall in little waves as the first-years are called together. Up ahead, Kōhei Sanada waits beside the lectern, perfectly still beneath the red academy crest. He lets the last scrape of a bench die away before he speaks.

“Good morning. From today, you are students of Phoenix Wing Academy. You will study Magic Theory, Magical Combat, and Potions and Alchemy. You will attend the lessons on your timetables. Being talented will not excuse being absent.”

A few shoulders straighten.

“You will also learn when to stop. A duel is not improved by an unnecessary injury. A useful spell is not improved by casting it where someone is eating. We expect effort, preparation, and the sense to ask when you do not understand.”

His gaze passes over the hall without lingering on anyone.

“Your first lesson is Magic Theory, in the Lecture Hall. Haruki Saitō is expecting you after this welcome. Follow the signs through the east doors. Good luck.”

Kōhei Sanada gathers his notes and returns toward the Faculty Offices. The formal silence breaks at once into voices, bags being lifted, and somebody discovering that a timetable can be upside down. Hinae Komori studies the arrow by the east doors, then gives it a small, satisfied nod.

Along the east corridor, a student board carries society notices, a few offers of paid afternoon help, and a small handbill pointing to the guild's public request board. None of it calls for a decision before class.

The Lecture Hall doors stand open. Haruki Saitō is setting a travel mug beside the board as first-years file through. The new student enters with the others, with the first lesson still ahead.

The cyan banners above Gryffin Tail's entrance barely move in the morning air. Everything below them is moving at once. Students with instrument cases weave around students with books; two returning classmates are arguing about a result neither has brought along. First-years gather near a desk in the Lecture Wing, where the registrar is steadily reducing a formidable stack of timetables.

The new student's name is already on the admitted list. A timetable changes hands, still faintly warm from the copying charm. Its morning blocks list the required rooms in order. Fumito Sakurai, wearing a welcome-duty ribbon over his second-year uniform, directs the newcomers toward the first-year welcome gathering with the concentration of someone determined not to provide three alternative routes.

“Straight ahead. The demonstrations can wait until this afternoon. That instruction is also for me.”

In the Lecture Wing’s welcome area, Nahlah Qamar turns her timetable to compare its headings with the schedule posted nearby, then carefully frees the end of her tail from beneath a bench. Around her, first-years gather for the headmaster’s address; the Lecture Hall waits farther along the wing.

Norio Shibata checks the wall clock and steps onto the low dais at the end of the welcome area.

“Good morning. Welcome to Gryffin Tail Academy. Your required subjects are Magic Theory, Magical Engineering, and Magical Arts. Please keep the timetable you have just received. The copy on the noticeboard is for reading, not taking.”

His delivery makes the final distinction sound thoroughly necessary.

“Lessons occupy the morning block. Restricted rooms remain restricted. If you find an error in a record, bring the record to the office. If you find an error in an experiment, tell the instructor before repeating it.”

He closes his folder.

“Kei Aoki will begin your first Magic Theory lesson in the Lecture Hall shortly. I will be in the Faculty Offices if an administrative matter needs correcting. I hope your first term goes well.”

The applause is brief but genuine. Norio Shibata heads toward the Faculty Offices, and the first-years begin moving toward their classroom.

Dragon Hoard's Arrival Gallery fills with yellow coats, gold-trimmed robes, luggage straps, and the smell of somebody's hastily purchased breakfast. Returning students pass the expedition exhibits without slowing. The new first-years slow down at nearly every case, until a member of staff waves them toward the timetable desk in the Exhibition Hall.

The new student's admission is already confirmed. The registrar finds the name, hands over a folded timetable, and points out the morning lesson block. On the next bench, Suzune Mikazuki is reading her own copy with the stern attention she usually reserves for judging whether something is tall enough to reach.

“The notices are at a sensible height this year,” she remarks. “A remarkable breakthrough.”

The first-years gather at the far end of the Exhibition Hall, where seats have been arranged for the welcome. Beyond the broad doorway, the gallery remains busy with older students heading to their own rooms. This is the start of the academic year for everyone, not a school waiting empty for one arrival.

Miyu Asahina stands at the front with a bright smile and one small stack of notes.

“Good morning, everyone. Welcome to Dragon Hoard Academy! You have your timetables, so you already know the most important thing: where somebody expects you to be.”

A little laughter travels through the benches.

“Magic Theory, Spellcraft, and Magical Creatures are your required subjects. Your lessons are in the morning. Please remember that wanting to investigate something is the beginning of a plan, rather than permission to open its case.”

She sets the notes down.

“You will learn how to ask useful questions, prepare for uncertain conditions, and bring discoveries home without losing the discovery or yourselves. First, though, you will learn the fundamentals. Noriaki Takatsuki is taking your Magic Theory lesson in the Lecture Hall shortly after we finish.”

Miyu Asahina looks across the first-year benches, pleased and quite serious beneath the warmth.

“Good luck. If your timetable is wrong, find me in the Faculty Offices. If you simply dislike the first bell, I sympathize. It is staying.”

Miyu Asahina gathers her notes and heads toward the Faculty Offices as the first-years rise and follow the signs to their classroom.

“Good morning. Welcome to Hydra Head Academy. You are now members of a school where many people share rooms, equipment, and the consequences of one another's decisions. We will try to make that a pleasant experience.”

Her pause leaves just enough room for a few uncertain smiles.

“Magic Theory, Enchantment, and Herbology are required subjects. Follow the morning lessons on your timetables. Keep track of announced practicals and examinations; a rumor that a practical has been cancelled is not an official notice.”

She rests one hand on the lectern.

“Your first Magic Theory lesson is with Kana Fujimoto in the Lecture Hall. The signs lead directly there. I will return to the Faculty Offices after this welcome. Good luck with your first morning.”

questGenerationGuidance.before:
OPPORTUNITIES AND AGREEMENT
Start with a person, concrete want and circumstance the player can act on. Reuse nearby authored people and acquaintances. A posting needs a client, terms and return contact. Offer two or three suitable possibilities when work is requested. Public news, overheard disagreements and visible problems can invite investigation without accepting or creating a journal entry. Ignore an unpursued lead rather than repeating it. Ordinary kindness and conversations need not become quests.

LOCAL CHARACTER
Academies: actual courses, teachers, years, experiments, contests, favors and rivalries. Their civic duties suggest work without dictating personality. The academic sequence keeps its own readiness and invitations.
Guild: finite contracts, hunts, escorts, recovery, repairs and professional disputes. Check the actual Bronze/Silver/Gold/Platinum badge. Pay the full posted fee; court keys and property permission remain separate.
Drakenspire: mountain routes, craft, clans, households, ancestors, pit contests and winter supplies. Terrain, promises and material needs create pressure; rare beings are not guaranteed appointments.
Asterveil: crossings, rescue, specimens, materials, research and competing expeditions. Distinguish Cloudbloom woodland, Rimeglass exposure, Mirrorwater channels and Amethyst acoustic terrain. Follow actual local bands and npcTypes; this remains midgame.
Everyday Glowhaven: food, music, neighbors, shopping, repairs and personal trouble. Simple work can end simply. Lawful prison work uses actual permission and never grants release just for finishing an errand.

PLAYABLE RESISTANCE
For substantial work, identify the obstacle, its location, how it blocks success and what resolves it. Use an actual rescue, contest, magical working, hazardous crossing, negotiation, fight or demonstrated result. Deliberately entering occupied dangerous ground produces the real encounter, not tracks forever. Tools, preparation, training and cooperation matter. Vary physical, magical, social and investigative approaches; animals are not negotiators by default.

QUESTS AND NATIVE ARCS
Most generated work is a finite standalone episode. Use configured arcs only for their actual premises, participants, secrets and expected conclusions; generated chapters belong to the runtime arc rather than an invented authored arcId. One meaningful development and its consequences justify another chapter. Preserve discoveries after a setback. Do not force every arc onto one player or split several simultaneous errands serving one goal into separate quests. Arc participants retain independent lives and motives. Respect credible alternative conclusions and do not restart a resolved arc merely to supply more content.

CHECKABLE ENDINGS
Give a generated quest a concrete final objective and a typed completionCondition repeating that final step's wording with the full relevant person, item and place names. Allow the stated alternatives and genuine imperfect results when appropriate. A proposal, quoted objective or unperformed promise does not qualify. Once achieved, let the scene show the deed plainly; no extra signatures, report loops or new mastermind are required. Failure can change cost, approach or relationships without erasing every clue.

CONTINUITY AND REWARDS
Compare active, planned, completed, declined and abandoned work by people, site and problem, not title alone. Preserve solved conditions; recurring work needs a fresh instance and terms. First thesis is once per playthrough, including transfers. Academic milestones, field tests, expeditions, the anomaly and Silken investigation retain separate conditions. No automatic calendar jump, acceptance, pass, recruitment or absent-participant credit.
State known risk, scope and payment before commitment. Respect refusal and withdrawal. Use one supported completion and reward owner; authored effects settle their fixed reward once. No duplicate prose payment or credit for unrelated work. Loans, salvage and customer property follow real agreements. Access, lessons and company can matter beside money; no generic reward grants affinity, mastery, court keys or affection.

INFORMED RISK
Routine work fits the least experienced human, excluding powerful NPC companions. Introductory Bronze work normally uses one level 1–3 weak hostile. Substantially harder work needs explicit player interest and concrete warning before acceptance. Offer a safer option instead of a surprise lethal mission. Existing scripted events, authored encounters and their conditions remain unchanged.

npcs.before:
STYLE FIRST
One striking hand-drawn 2D fantasy-anime character illustration: crisp ink lines with deliberate weight variation, expressive anime eyes, clean hair masses, graphic cel-shaded shadow shapes and vibrant controlled color. Flashy key-visual finish with readable design and selective effects. Faces are anime drawings with simplified nose and cheek planes, clean skin and clear irises; keep edges drawn, not beveled or sculpted.

PLAYER DIRECTION
If supplied player Appearance begins with ## GLOWHAVEN PLAYER PORTRAIT, use that complete visual brief and the selected optional portrait choices. A compatible explicit player composition takes priority. Skipped choices use the defaults below. A visual style or background creates no powers, items, property, affiliation or travel.

IDENTITY
Preserve the actual face, apparent age, skin, eye and hair colors, hairstyle, build, outfit, selected accessories and species anatomy. A selected bald or shaved scalp has no invented head hair. Follow authored visualDescription and selected individual features rather than a stock beauty. Adults retain adult proportions; youthful long-lived people keep their established presentation. Beastfolk are mostly human in face and body with only their specified ears, horns, tails or other animal details; rare more animal-like bodies require explicit direction. Fae have their actual individual wings, hooves, antlers or bark scales, not a universal fairy body. A short fae is still an adult. Nonhumanoids keep their actual anatomy.

FRAME AND EXPRESSION
Default to a vertical waist-up or hip-up portrait, complete head and hairstyle visible, a clear expression and enough costume to read the silhouette. For a marked player portrait, an explicit selected crop or viewpoint overrides this default, including bust, face close-up, full-body and dramatic perspective. Use comfortable natural space above the head, without a fixed percentage. Default eye-level or three-quarter view; vary body turn, gaze, gesture and supported posture. Optional camera and crop choices are welcome. Do not default every person to standing squarely or holding a focus upright. Hands and gear must connect coherently; a long staff may extend outside the crop.

GEAR AND SETTING
Show actual equipment and fitting clothing. Use ability-consistent effects where appropriate, keeping the face readable; a novice’s visual flair does not grant mastery. Use a selected picture backdrop or a few recognizable cues from the opening/current place, in the same drawn style. A stylized graphic backdrop is valid when selected. Background remains secondary. Keep individual palette variety. Academy accents: Phoenix Wing red, Gryffin Tail cyan, Dragon Hoard gold, Hydra Head violet.

AVOID
3D render, CGI, photorealism, semi-realistic faces, live action, photographic skin texture, plastic shine, sculpted cheekbones, bevelled edges, ray tracing, doll faces, photographic hair, bokeh smearing, overpainted muddy lines, extra limbs, wrong anatomy, recolored eyes, invented equipment, unintentional face clipping or an unrequested distant view. Explicit player framing can deliberately crop outer hair or hat edges, or show the whole body. No text, lettering, captions, logos, signature, watermark, borders, character sheets or interface. One focal character only.

before.name: Guild: Adventurer Licensure
before.questStatement: The guild accepts martial and magical applicants. Registration opens an assessment; a real pass earns the first Bronze badge.
before.mainObjective: Pass the judgment and practical portions, then receive certification at the counter.
before.questDesignBrief:
Offer on an actual application, not every first visit. Explain judgment, declared scope, retreat and practical control. Let the applicant use their real trained weapon, body technique, magic or mixed method in a bounded safe exercise; no universal Intelligence test or compulsory spell. A real check and the supplied outcome determine practical success. A capable newcomer may demonstrate competence promptly; failing is a reason to practice, not humiliation or arbitrary detention. Komugi Hanabishi handles the docket and certification; an appropriate duty assessor may supervise practical work. Personal pass records and the actual issuance trigger control the badge. No starting badge, free weapon, portal key or automatic pass from level. Registration/assessment adds no invented charge. Applicants can postpone or leave.
The certification trigger exclusively awards the existing Document Guild Badge: Bronze. Do not also put a badge in generated quest rewards or create a renamed Relic for the same licence.

judgment.text: Pass the request-reading and practical-judgment review.

practical.text: Complete a controlled practical demonstration with your trained method.

certify.text: Have the completed results certified at reception.
